newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-PAKISTAN BATSMEN AWAIT ORDERS ON LOGOS.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-PAKISTAN BATSMEN AWAIT ORDERS ON LOGOS.

text.p: Pakistan batsmen are awaiting orders from their cricket board before removing tobacco logos from their bats, the team manager said on Friday, despite an order by the Australian government to remove the slogans.
Manager Yawar Saeed said he had notified the Pakistan Cricket Board and was awaiting their decision.
"I'm not the policy-maker so I will have to wait until I get the new instructions," Saeed told Australian radio.
However, it was unlikely the logos would be removed before Friday's World Series day-night match against the West Indies in Brisbane, as Friday was a public holiday in Pakistan, he said.
Pakistan is scheduled to play Australia in a one-day match on Sunday in Brisbane.

The Australian government on Thursday gave Pakistan until next Tuesday to remove the Wills King cigarette company slogan from bats used by the team under strict laws banning cigarette advertising in sport.

The logos were visible on bats used by a number of Pakistan players during the touring team's four-wicket defeat of Australia in a World Series match in Sydney on Wednesday. The match was televised around Australia and internationally.
The Australian government notified the Australian Cricket Board (ACB) of its decision on Thursday and it in turn notified the Pakistan manager.
Saeed said the ACB did not recommend any action.
"They (the ACB) are awaiting the response from the Pakistan Cricket Board," he said. The ACB faces a fine of A$60,000 (US$47,400) unless Pakistan removes the logos.
Saeed said he did not whether the Pakistan Cricket Board would comply with the order.
"If we knew that we were violating (advertising laws) we would not do it. We do not violate rules of our own country or any other country," he said.
"We will just continue doing what we are told to do."

Many of the Pakistan players, who are in Australia for the World Series limited overs tournament against Australia and West Indies, have stickers bearing the corporate logo and name of team sponsors Wills Kings, a Pakistani company which manufactures cricket equipment and cigarettes.
A spokesman for Australia's health minister said on Thursday the team must adhere to strict rules on tobacco advertising.

Tobacco adverts are banned at Australian sporting and cultural events unless an exemption is granted under the Tobacco Advertising Prohibition Act. The Formula One Grand Prix motor race in Victoria next March has such an exemption.
